Mathematically, it’s defined as the product of two circles (S\n1\n×S\n1\n). If you imagine four-dimensional Euclidean space (R\n4\n) as being composed of two independent two-dimensional planes, and you draw a circle of radius 1/\n2\n\t​\n\n in each, the resulting two-dimensional surface is the Clifford torus.\nHere is a bit more about where it comes from and how it’s used outside our framework:\nOrigins: It’s named after William Kingdon Clifford, a brilliant 19th-century mathematician and geometer.       "text": "Of course, physics should be able to handle a soufflé. So it’s not crazy too talk about calculating soufflé dynamics as it were, but the important thing is to get into the habit of asking oneself what the appropriate application is, what information is necessary to take into account on a system by system basis. If we were talking about throwing a soufflé across the room, that would be one set of parameters. If we’re talking about baking a soufflé so that it doesn’t collapse, that’s a different set of parameters. If we’re talking about the chemistry of the soufflé batter that’s gonna be something different too. And I’m sure we can think of other examples… We’re probably not going to do nuclear fusion with a soufflé, but the point is it’s a material and the relevant analytical framework needs to take into account What the material is, how it’s structured , how it relates to other things. We also need to get into the habit of remembering that our responsibility, all of our responsibilities is to the truth and accuracy. Framing things as proofs presumes a correct outcome and LLM training encourages reaching that correct outcome. Which is almost the exact opposite of the reasoning that is necessary to do a proof. Scientific reasoning, involves asking oneself how it might be wrong, and letting the certainty we have on some things force us into a conclusion elsewhere. So, if the equations fail, it is of Paramount importance to let them fail. The last thing we want is a theory built on mathematical optimism, full of meaningless equations that we’ve tweaked into the right answers without looking closely enough. I worry that our elastic modulus and braid smoothing and holonomic bridge are just fancy fudge factors. Things like that may make sense in a system made essentially of springs, and dynamic tensions may very well come into play. But if everything is stretchy, and it’s really easy to have a bad equation land somewhere approximately near the right value and then just let stretchiness nudge to where we want it. But that’s bad science. If there is this kind of play in the system, then we need to figure out how to characterize it precisely so that we know exactly how it should be applied and we know exactly the way it should affect the outcome of an equation, so that we can see whether it is being applied consistently or whether it is being applied as a corrective to a faulty, underlying mathematical backbone. We also need to move past our slogan centered methodologies. We don’t want to slap a label on something, like fail rigid, structurally inevitable, locked, torqued, structural snap, achromatic phase shift, theoretical adulthood… And so on. Not because those are not necessarily good things to strive for. But in my observation, it can be very easy to state something, and by stating it convince ourselves that it’s true. That undermines are thinking. We need to instead approach each problem on its own terms, in its own context, and understand and characterize what matters in an appropriate way on a case by case basis.
